study.title: Ezekiel 3 - Word received, difficult mission and responsibility to warn
study.overview: Ezekiel 3 shows the prophet being prepared by God for a hard mission among his own people. First, he receives the divine word as food: the scroll is sweet when it is eaten, indicating that hearing and accepting the message of God is good, even when the content includes judgment. Then God sends him to Israel, a people who did not want to hear, and strengthens him not to fear opposition. Then Ezekiel is taken by the Spirit to the exiles and is silent for seven days, until he receives the watchman's commission: he must warn the wicked and the righteous, because the silence before sin brings guilt. Finally, God restricts and also restores the prophet's speech: he will only speak when God opens his mouth, making it clear that the message belongs to the Lord and that the human answer is heard or reject - will be with every hearer.

outline.title: The Word of God as Sweet Food
outline.explanation: Ezekiel receives the roll and eats it. The experience is inside: the message needs to be assimilated before it is announced. The roll is sweet in the mouth, showing that receiving the word of God is, in itself, a joy, even when the advertised content will not be easy.

outline.title: Sending Israel and the Resistance of the People
outline.explanation: God sends him specifically to the house of Israel, which is described as stubborn and hard-hearted. The prophet receives courage to face rejection. The Spirit leads him to the exiles, where he abides seven asymptotic days, with inner bitterness, but under the strong hand of the Lord.

outline.title: The commission of watchman and the fault of omission
outline.explanation: After seven days God set up Ezekiel as a watchman. If he does not warn the wicked, he will be responsible for his blood; if he warns and the person does not repent, the prophet will be free. The same responsibility also applies to the righteous who deviates: the duty of the messenger is to warn faithfully.

outline.title: Silence imposed and speaks restored by God
outline.explanation: In the valley Ezekiel sees the glory of the Lord again. The Spirit puts him up and God sends him to gather, becoming silent until the Lord himself opens his mouth. Thus, the prophet does not speak on his own initiative: he announces only when God gives him word, summarized in the call to listen or to refusal.

study.context: The chapter shows Ezekiel among the exiles, near the river Chebar, and mentions Tel-Abibe. The text also suggests a seven-day interval in which the prophet remains among the captives, in silence and astonishment, before receiving the new commission. Matthew Henry's notes note that this period may have coincided with the seventh day; this is a devotional inference, not an explicit given from the verse. The setting is that of a people already in captivity, but still responsible for hearing the word of the Lord.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that the word of God should be received before it is proclaimed: the messenger needs to internalize the message, not just repeat it. He also states that human resistance does not nullify divine authority; the prophet speaks in the name of the Lord, whether they hear, or stop hearing. There is still a strong theology of responsibility: to warn is a serious duty, and silence before sin can make the messenger guilty. At the same time, God sovereignly sustains his servant, giving him courage, restricting his speech and opening it when he pleases. The result is that the authority of the message rests on God, while the listener's response remains a moral decision before the divine voice.

scholarViews.insight: The roll is sweet when being eaten, showing that accepting the word of God is pleasing to the prophet, even when the content of the message includes judgment.
The mission of the watchman shows that the prophet must warn faithfully; the omission makes him responsible for the guilt of those who have not been warned.
The language of Ezekiel is restricted to God to open his mouth; he speaks only when the Lord authorizes him, and the final answer belongs to the listener.

questions: What does it mean, in practice, to "become" the word of God before enforcing it to others?
In what ways can heart hardness appear today, even among people who know the language of faith?
How can we take seriously the responsibility of admonishing without losing humility and compassion?
study.practice: Set time to read Scripture not only for information, but for assimilation and obedience. Before speaking of God to other people, ask the Word to first mold his heart. Also examine if there is any sin that you have avoided confronting yourself or someone close by: when there is opportunity and responsibility, it may come with meekness and clarity, remembering that the result belongs to the Lord. Finally, practice listening: not every rejection of the truth will be resolved by arguments; some will require perseverance, prayer and courage.
study.uncertainty: Some details of the immediate historical context are not explained in the chapter and therefore cannot be affirmed accurately beyond what the text itself and the notes say. Matthew Henry's observation of the seventh day as possible Saturday is a probable interpretation, not a textual certainty. Adam Clarke's notes on the possibility of the just falling and perish represent his theological reading; the chapter affirms the responsibility of the watchman, but does not define here all the doctrinal debates on perseverance.
